cim_eredeti: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds
szoveg_eredeti:
(function(){var r=document.getElementById("pp-google-row");var m=document.querySelector(".jeg_meta_container");if(r&&m&&m.parentNode){m.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",r);}})();People tend to perceive artificial intelligence systems as White, even when those systems lack a face, voice, name, or body, according to new research published in Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Across a series of studies, this racial association was linked to greater trust in AI recommendations, and systems described as trained on data from Black and Latino adults were assigned less intellectually demanding work than identical systems trained on White or unspecified data. The findings indicate that human users project familiar social hierarchies onto emerging technologies, which may shape how much authority people grant to automated tools.

Racialization is the psychological process of assigning a racial identity and its accompanying cultural stereotypes to an entity, practice, or concept that has no inherent biological race. Most public and scientific discussions of racial bias in artificial intelligence focus on how software programs treat different groups of people, such as facial recognition tools that misidentify darker skin tones or lending algorithms that penalize minority applicants. Less attention has been paid to the reverse question: whether human users view disembodied software programs, such as chatbots and recommendation engines, as possessing a racial identity of their own.

“This research grew out of a question about an assumption we often make about technology: that it’s somehow neutral or separate from the social biases and hierarchies that shape human society,” study lead author Monica Gamez-Djokic, an assistant professor of psychological sciences at Purdue University, told PsyPost. “If we routinely interpret other people through social categories like race, might we do the same with AI, even when it has no obvious racial identity? And if so, could those perceptions shape how much we trust AI or value its recommendations?”

The new research, conducted by Gamez-Djokic alongside Adam Waytz of Northwestern University, builds on the psychological concept of anthropomorphism, which is the human tendency to attribute minds, intentions, and personalities to non-human objects. Once people treat a responsive computer program like a social partner, their brains automatically apply the same mental shortcuts used to categorize human beings, sorting the entity by social traits like gender, age, and race. Even concepts without any physical form can acquire racial associations; for example, a series of experiments with U.S. adults found that people both explicitly and implicitly associate vegetarianism with White people, a stereotype that reduced feelings of belonging in the vegetarian community among Black adults.

Don’t miss the next big psychology finding

Every morning, PsyPost sends a short briefing on the most interesting new peer-reviewed research in psychology and neuroscience.

Gamez-Djokic and Waytz proposed two main reasons why abstract AI systems might specifically be categorized as White. First, in Western cultures, Whiteness often operates as an unstated default identity and is stereotypically linked with high status, technical expertise, and intelligence, allowing stereotypes about intelligence to spill over onto smart technologies. Second, the authors suggested that people make inferences based on the broader ecosystem surrounding AI, forming impressions based on who they believe programs the software, who uses it, and whose knowledge is fed into its training data.

If people view AI through a racial lens, those perceptions could alter how they evaluate its advice in workplaces and daily life. In many U.S. studies, White speakers have been judged as more objective and competent than non-White speakers delivering the exact same message. Understanding what drives confidence in automated advice is increasingly relevant as organizations adopt these tools; for instance, a 2026 survey of organizational employees indicated that higher trust in AI decision-support systems is associated with a greater intention to rely on them and with people reporting that they put less effort into evaluating decisions themselves.

To test their hypotheses, the researchers conducted five primary studies and eight supplementary studies. The five primary studies were preregistered, as were some of the supplementary studies, and data, code, and materials for all of them were posted publicly on the Open Science Framework. In Study 1a, the team recruited 459 U.S. adults through CloudResearch, equally balanced across White, Black, Asian, and Hispanic or Latino participants, who indicated which racial or ethnic group from a standard list they associated with six technologies: AI, a machine learning algorithm, a robot, a computer, a chatbot, and a self-driving car.

Because forcing participants to pick from a preset list of racial labels might artificially manufacture racial judgments, the researchers changed the format in Study 1b. A separate racially balanced sample of 465 U.S. adults on Prolific answered the same question for the six technologies using an open-ended text box, allowing them to write in whatever response they wished. Independent coders then evaluated whether participants named a race and whether that race was White.

In Study 1a, participants selected White for 72% of the technologies on average, well above the 50% benchmark the researchers tested against. That is a conservative comparison, since participants could choose from six categories. In Study 1b, participants spontaneously assigned a racial identity to 75% of the technologies they evaluated, and among those racialized responses, 71% were described as White. In both studies, this pattern held regardless of the participant’s own racial background, and a supplementary study that added an explicit “no race” button showed that participants who chose a race were still more likely to pick White.

Because Studies 1a and 1b directly asked participants to think about race, the authors designed Study 2 to test whether people also hold an implicit, unspoken mental image of AI as White when race is never mentioned. They used a two-phase reverse-correlation task, a technique that reconstructs what a concept looks like in a person’s imagination. In the first phase, 96 participants from the Chicago community viewed 300 pairs of blurry faces, created by layering random visual static over a neutral base photograph of a European male face, and picked which image in each pair looked more like “artificial intelligence.”

The researchers digitally averaged all the selected images into a single composite “AI face” and averaged all the rejected images into a comparison “anti-face.” In the second phase, a separate group of 172 participants, who did not know how the portraits had been created, identified the race of both composite images. In that phase, 75% of raters categorized the composite AI face as White, compared to 43% for the rejected anti-face, suggesting that participants’ selections pushed the visual representation toward stereotypically White facial features.

“What surprised me most was how little information people needed to racialize AI,” Gamez-Djokic said. “In our initial studies, the technologies had no faces, voices, names, or other obvious racial cues, yet participants consistently associated them with Whiteness.”

“I found this interesting because much of the research on how people respond socially to technology focuses on what happens when we make machines more humanlike,” she added. “Our findings suggest that people may bring human social categories to AI even when those humanlike features are absent.”

To see whether this tendency was strictly an American phenomenon, Study 3 expanded the categorization task to English-speaking adults living in India (147 participants) and Japan (113 participants).
